What lies behind the seductive power of Art? 
Alfred Gell puts forward a theory that departs 
radically from previous interpretations of art. 
He argues that aesthetic theories take an over- 
whelmingly passive perspective on the art object 
and puts emphasis instead upon art as a form of 
instrumental action: the making of things as a 
means of influencing the thoughts and actions 
of others. Art objects embody complex inten- 
tionalities and mediate social agency; persons 
_and art objects merge together in his 
conceptualization. Gell explores the psychology 
of patterns and perception; art and personhood; 
art in its relations with religious practices. 
including spirit possession, idolatory, and 
Christian church services; the meaning of art 
for the artist, the gallery-goer, and the idolater. 
Gell’s argument develops through detailed discussion of theoretical issues 
belonging to philosophy, psychology, and linguistics. It is enriched by diverse

illustrations and an analysis of European and ‘ethnographic’ art. 
Art and Agency was completed just before Alfred Gell’s death at the age of 51 in 
January 1997. It embodies the intellectual bravura, lively wit, vigour, and erudition 
for which he was admired, and will stand as an enduring testament to one of the 
. 
most gifted anthropologists of his generation.

“This is a remarkable work . 
. 
. witty, elegant, broad in its compass and scintillating 
in its detail. 
. 
. 
. The book knows what to do with the limits of form—one suddenly 
sees how anthropology might surpass itself.’ 
Marilyn Strathern FBA, Professor of Anthropology, University of Cambridge 
‘An extraordinary achievement. Gell offers a profound new understanding of 
collective agency which completely reshapes the anthropology of art, redefines its 
objects of study, and inspires new conclusions.’ 
Caroline Humphrey, Reader in Asian Anthropology, University of Cambridge 
“This book changes the very basis of the way art has been viewed in the human 
sciences. 
. 
. 
. Its publication is a major event.’ 
Maurice Bloch FBA, Professor of Anthropology, London School of Economies 
Alfred Gell was Reader in Anthropology at the London School of Economics 
and Political Science, and was a Fellow of the British Academy. The School 
posthumously awarded him a Professorship, a post that he had declined during his 
lifetime. He published three books in his lifetime: Metamorphosis of the Cassowaries 
(1975), The Anthropology of Time (1992), and Wrapping in Images: Tattooing in 
Polynesia (1993).
